﻿# Precedent: Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc.
COURT: Supreme Court of the United States
CITATION: 510 U.S. 569 (1994)
DATE: 1994-03-07
JURISDICTION: US Federal / Copyright

## Facts
2 Live Crew created a parody rap song based on Roy Orbison and William Dees's copyrighted rock ballad "Oh, Pretty Woman". Acuff-Rose Music sued 2 Live Crew for copyright infringement after refusing to grant a license.

## Legal Issue
Whether 2 Live Crew's commercial parody constitutes fair use under Section 107 of the Copyright Act of 1976.

metadata.title: precedent_campbell_v_acuff_rose.md
metadata.court: Supreme Court of the United States

text:
using to grant a license.

## Legal Issue
Whether 2 Live Crew's commercial parody constitutes fair use under Section 107 of the Copyright Act of 1976. ## Holding and Judicial Reasoning
Justice Souter delivered the opinion of the unanimous Court:
1. Parody, like other comment or criticism, may claim fair use under Section 107.
2. The enquiry under § 107(1) focuses on whether the new work merely supersedes the objects of the original creation, or instead adds something new, with a further purpose or different character; in other words, whether and to what extent the new work is "transformative".
3. The threshold question when fair use is invoked in a parody is whether a parodic character may reasonably be perceived.
4. Commercial purpose is only one element to be weighed in a fair use inquiry and does not create an irrebuttable presumption against fair use.

﻿# Precedent: Hadley v Baxendale
COURT: Court of Exchequer (England & Wales)
CITATION: (1854) 9 Exch 341, 156 Eng. Rep. 145
DATE: 1854-02-23
JURISDICTION: Common Law / Commercial Contracts

## Facts
Plaintiffs operated a flour mill in Gloucester. The crankshaft of the steam engine broke, causing the mill to stop. Plaintiffs engaged Defendant Baxendale, a common carrier, to transport the broken shaft to engineers in Greenwich to serve as a pattern for a new shaft. Defendant's servant promised delivery within two days. Due to Defendant's neglect, delivery was delayed for seven days, during which the mill remained idle and lost substantial profits.

ry within two days. Due to Defendant's neglect, delivery was delayed for seven days, during which the mill remained idle and lost substantial profits. ## Legal Issue
Whether a common carrier can be held liable for consequential lost business profits resulting from delivery delays when the carrier was not expressly informed that the entire operation of the mill was halted awaiting the replacement.

resulting from delivery delays when the carrier was not expressly informed that the entire operation of the mill was halted awaiting the replacement. ## Holding and Rule of Law
Where two parties have made a contract which one of them has broken, the damages which the other party ought to receive in respect of such breach of contract should be such as may fairly and reasonably be considered either arising naturally, i.e., according to the usual course of things, from such breach of contract itself, or such as may reasonably be supposed to have been in the contemplation of both parties, at the time they made the contract, as the probable result of the breach of it.

sonably be supposed to have been in the contemplation of both parties, at the time they made the contract, as the probable result of the breach of it. Special or consequential damages are recoverable only if the special circumstances were communicated to and known by both parties at the formation of the agreement.

# Precedent: Lawson v. FMR LLC
COURT: Supreme Court of the United States
CITATION: 571 U.S. 429 (2014)
DATE: 2014-03-04
JURISDICTION: US Federal / Whistleblower Protection

## Facts
Plaintiffs Jackie Hosang Lawson and Jonathan M. Zang were former employees of FMR LLC (Fidelity Investments), private companies that contract with the Fidelity family of mutual funds to provide investment management services. Mutual funds themselves are public companies with no employees of their own; they contract out all operations. Plaintiffs alleged that after raising concerns about cost-accounting methodologies and mutual fund registration statements, they suffered unlawful retaliation resulting in constructive discharge.

s about cost-accounting methodologies and mutual fund registration statements, they suffered unlawful retaliation resulting in constructive discharge. ## Legal Issue
Whether Section 806 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (18 U.S.C. § 1514A), which prohibits retaliation against an "employee" who reports corporate fraud, shelters employees of private contractors and subcontractors that advise or serve public mutual funds.

metadata.title: precedent_lawson_v_fmr.md
metadata.court: Supreme Court of the United States

text:
inst an "employee" who reports corporate fraud, shelters employees of private contractors and subcontractors that advise or serve public mutual funds. ## Holding and Rule of Law
Justice Ginsburg delivered the opinion of the Court (6-3):
1. Whistleblower protection under 18 U.S.C. § 1514A extends to employees of contractors and subcontractors of public companies, including employees of private investment advisers who manage public mutual funds.
2. The ordinary meaning of "an employee" who may not be discriminated against by "any contractor, subcontractor, or agent" includes the contractor's own employees.
3. Congress enacted SOX in direct response to the Enron collapse, where outside contractors (auditors, law firms, accounting partners) were deeply implicated in concealing corporate malfeasance. Protecting contractor employees is essential to preventing retaliatory silencing of insiders who uncover shareholder fraud.

# Precedent: Van Buren v. United States
COURT: Supreme Court of the United States
CITATION: 593 U.S. 374 (2021)
DATE: 2021-06-03
JURISDICTION: US Federal / Computer Fraud & Cyber Law

## Facts
Nathan Van Buren, a former police sergeant in Georgia, accepted an illicit cash payment to search a state license plate database (the Criminal Justice Information Services database) for an individual in exchange for personal financial gain. Van Buren had valid credentials and legitimate administrative access to the database as part of his police duties, but accessed the record for an unauthorized personal/improper purpose in violation of police department policy.

metadata.court: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.jurisdiction: US Federal / Computer Fraud & Cyber Law

text:
database as part of his police duties, but accessed the record for an unauthorized personal/improper purpose in violation of police department policy. ## Legal Issue
Whether a person "exceeds authorized access" under Section 1030(a)(2) of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act by accessing computer information with valid credentials but for an improper or unauthorized purpose.

metadata.title: precedent_van_buren_v_us.md
metadata.court: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.jurisdiction: US Federal / Computer Fraud & Cyber Law

text:
n 1030(a)(2) of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act by accessing computer information with valid credentials but for an improper or unauthorized purpose. ## Holding and Rule of Law
Justice Barrett delivered the opinion of the Court (6-3):
1. An individual "exceeds authorized access" under 18 U.S.C. § 1030(e)(6) when he accesses a computer with authorization and then obtains information located in particular areas of the computer (such as files, folders, or databases) that are off-limits to him.
2. The CFAA does NOT cover an individual who has lawful administrative credentials to access information stored on a computer, even if that individual accesses that information for an improper purpose or in violation of corporate employment policies.
3. The statute establishes a "gates-up / gates-down" technological inquiry: either the technological system authorizes the user to enter that directory, or it does not. Purpose-based contractual violations (e.g. Terms of Service, employee handbooks) do not constitute unauthorized access under federal cyber law.

﻿# Illustrative Case: Apex Logistics Solutions LLC v. Horizon Retail Enterprise Inc.
CASE_ID: CASE-2025-001
JURISDICTION: Delaware Commercial Court / Common Law
DATE_FILED: 2025-01-15

## Summary of Dispute
Horizon Retail Enterprise Inc. entered into a Master Logistics Service Agreement with Apex Logistics Solutions LLC on June 1, 2024. Horizon operates 45 retail stores and an online e-commerce platform. Apex contracted to provide dedicated fulfillment and refrigerated linehaul distribution.

Paragraph 14.2 of the Agreement stated:
'In the event Apex fails to deliver designated shipments within the guaranteed 48-hour delivery window, Apex shall pay liquidated damages of $5,000 per delayed truckload per day, regardless of actual loss.'

Between November 20 and November 28, 2024 (peak holiday shopping week), Apex suffered fleet driver shortages and routing software outages. Six critical linehaul shipments were delayed by 4 days. Horizon withheld payments totaling $120,000 claiming liquidated damages under Paragraph 14.2. Horizon also claimed an additional $350,000 in lost customer goodwill and lost sales.

2. The delay was caused by an unprecedented third-party cloud outage affecting telematics (arguing force majeure / commercial impracticability).

(1) Damages for breach by either party may be liquidated in the agreement but only at an amount that is reasonable in the light of the anticipated or actual loss caused by the breach and the difficulties of proof of loss. A term fixing unreasonably large liquidated damages is unenforceable on grounds of public policy as a penalty.
(2) A term in a bond providing for an amount of money as a penalty for non-occurrence of the condition of the bond is unenforceable on grounds of public policy to the extent that the amount exceeds the loss caused by such non-occurrence.

DATE: 2016-05-11 DEFINITIONS AND MISAPPROPRIATION OF TRADE SECRETS
Under 18 U.S.C. § 1839(3), the term "trade secret" means all forms and types of financial, business, scientific, technical, economic, or engineering information, including patterns, plans, compilations, program devices, formulas, designs, prototypes, methods, techniques, processes, procedures, programs, or codes, whether tangible or intangible, and whether or how stored, compiled, or memorialized physically, electronically, graphically, photographically, or in writing if:
(A) the owner thereof has taken reasonable measures to keep such information secret; and
(B) the information derives independent economic value, actual or potential, from not being generally known to, and not being readily ascertainable through proper means by, another person who can obtain economic value from the disclosure or use of the information.

d not being readily ascertainable through proper means by, another person who can obtain economic value from the disclosure or use of the information. MISAPPROPRIATION DEFINED
Under 18 U.S.C. § 1839(5), misappropriation entails:
(A) acquisition of a trade secret of another by a person who knows or has reason to know that the trade secret was acquired by improper means; or
(B) disclosure or use of a trade secret of another without express or implied consent by a person who used improper means to acquire knowledge of the trade secret, or knew at the time of disclosure or use that knowledge of the trade secret was derived through a person who had utilized improper means or acquired under circumstances giving rise to a duty to maintain secrecy.

TITLE: Sarbanes-Oxley Act - Section 806 (Whistleblower Protection)
JURISDICTION: US Federal
DOCUMENT_TYPE: Statute
CITATION: 18 U.S.C. § 1514A
DATE: 2002-07-30

SECTION 1514A: CIVIL ACTION TO PROTECT AGAINST RETALIATION IN FRAUD CASES
(a) In General - No company with a class of securities registered under section 12 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, or that is required to file reports under section 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, including any contractor, subcontractor, or agent of such company, may discharge, demote, suspend, threaten, harass, or in any other manner discriminate against an employee in the terms and conditions of employment because of any lawful act done by the employee:
(1) to provide information, cause information to be provided, or otherwise assist in an investigation regarding any conduct which the employee reasonably believes constitutes a violation of section 1341 (mail fraud), 1343 (wire fraud), 1344 (bank fraud), or 1348 (securities fraud), any rule or regulation of the Securities and Exchange Commission, or any provision of Federal law relating to fraud against shareholders, when the information or assistance is provided to:
  (A) a Federal regulatory or law enforcement agency;
  (B) any Member of Congress or any committee of Congress; or
  (C) a person with supervisory authority over the employee.
